objectives: Describe how an anti-lock braking system works and what its parts do.
Name the terms of braking: braking distance, traction, lock-up, threshold braking and brake fade.
Explain where ABS does not help, and why the surface decides the answer.
Compare threshold braking, progressive braking, engine braking and braking with ABS.
Use the right braking method on a firm surface, on loose ground and on ice.
Follow the steps of braking well in a car with ABS and in a car without it.
Say what to do when the ABS warning light comes on.

sections.body:
Anti-lock braking is a system on the brakes of a car. It watches the wheels and keeps them turning when the driver brakes hard enough to lock one of them. A locked wheel skids: the tyre slides instead of gripping, the car does not slow as well as it could, and the steering goes away. With anti-lock braking the wheel keeps turning, so the driver can steer the car around an obstacle while the car slows.

Five words carry the subject. **Braking distance** is the distance the car travels from the moment the driver touches the brake to the moment the car stops. **Traction** is the grip between the tyre and the road, and it is what turns the car's speed into a stop. **Lock-up** is the moment a wheel stops turning while the car is still moving. **Threshold braking** is the driver's own way of braking at the limit, just before lock-up, by pressing and releasing the pedal. **Brake fade** is the loss of braking power when the brakes get hot, so that the pedal goes soft and the car takes longer to stop.

What the system does not do is shorten the braking distance on every surface. On a firm road the anti-lock system usually stops the car in a shorter distance than a locked wheel would. On loose gravel, sand, mud, snow or leaves, a locked wheel can dig into the surface and give the shorter stop, and the system, which insists on keeping the wheel turning, can leave the car rolling further than the driver expects.

The system was developed to keep the wheel turning so that the driver can steer. That is the whole of it. It is not a promise that the car always stops in the same distance, and it never gives the driver more grip than the road has.
examples: The anti-lock system keeps the wheel turning, so I can steer the car while it slows.
The braking distance is the distance from the pedal to the stop; the time before that is the reaction time.
On gravel a locked wheel can be the shorter stop, so I ease the brake there.
A hot brake fades, and the pedal goes soft.
sections.heading: What anti-lock braking is, and what it is not

terms.example: The car has an anti-lock braking system, so I press the pedal and keep it down.
terms.gloss: A system on the brakes that keeps the wheels turning when the driver brakes hard, so that the car can still be steered.

terms.example: On a wet road the braking distance is longer than on a dry road.
terms.gloss: The distance the car travels from the moment the driver touches the brake to the moment the car stops.

terms.example: There is little traction on ice, so the car slides even at a low speed.
terms.gloss: The grip between the tyre and the road, and it is what turns the car's speed into a stop.

terms.example: The front wheel went into lock-up and the steering went light.
terms.gloss: The moment when a wheel stops turning while the car is still moving.

terms.example: Without ABS the driver has to use threshold braking.
terms.gloss: Braking at the limit of grip by pressing and releasing the pedal before the wheel locks.

terms.example: After the long descent the brakes faded and the pedal felt weak.
terms.gloss: The loss of braking power when the brakes are hot, so that the pedal goes soft.

sections.body:
Four parts do the work: a sensor at each wheel, a control unit, a modulator, and the brake itself. The **sensor** is a small part at each wheel that reports how fast that wheel is turning. The **control unit** compares the rotation of the four wheels with each other, and it compares them with the speed of the car. When one wheel is turning much more slowly than the others while the car is still moving, that wheel is on its way to locking.

The control unit then tells the **modulator** to change the brake pressure at that wheel. The pressure can be reduced, so that the wheel turns again, held, so that the wheel stays just at the limit of locking, or increased, so that the brake takes more of the work. The modulator does this again and again, many times a second, and the driver never sees it.

The brake is never switched off. This is the point that is often misunderstood: the system manages the pressure, it does not take the brake away. The pedal stays down, the brake stays applied, and the system keeps the wheel turning inside that applied brake. The driver must therefore keep the pedal pressed firmly and keep the steering steady.

The pedal tells the driver what is happening. In a hard stop with the system working, the pedal pulses under the foot. That pulse is the modulator changing the pressure. It is not a fault, and it is not a reason to let the pedal up.
examples: The sensor on each wheel reports the rotation, and the control unit compares the wheels with each other.
The modulator reduces the pressure at the wheel that is about to lock.
The brake stays applied: the system manages the pressure, it does not switch the brake off.
sections.heading: How the system decides how hard to brake

terms.example: A damaged sensor at one wheel can switch the ABS off.
terms.gloss: A small part at each wheel that reports how fast that wheel is turning.

terms.example: The modulator holds the pressure at the wheel that is about to lock.
terms.gloss: The part of the brake that changes the brake pressure at a wheel when the system asks it to.

sections.body:
Anti-lock braking is a system for a firm surface. On loose gravel, sand, mud, snow and fallen leaves, the material under the tyre moves and the tyre sinks into it. A locked wheel ploughs through the loose material and digs a trench, and on these surfaces it can stop the car in a shorter distance than a wheel that keeps turning, so the system can leave the car rolling further than the driver expects. A damaged tyre changes the answer as well: a tyre with a deep cut, a bulge or a cut in the sidewall can lose its grip or come apart under load, and an under-inflated tyre cannot put its full tread on the road. The system cannot repair a tyre; it manages the brake pressure around whatever the tyre is doing.

On ice, the limit is the friction between the tyre and the road, not the braking system. Both a locked wheel and a turning wheel can only ask the ice for what the ice has. Anti-lock braking helps the driver keep the steering, and it does not add grip that is not there.

A motorcycle is a different machine. The front brake carries more of the work, the rider's balance matters, and the technique on a bike is not the technique in a car. Some motorcycles have anti-lock braking and some do not; for the rider the answers are training and the manual of the bike.

A long descent is a heat problem. A brake slows a car by turning movement into heat, and heat that stays in the brake has nowhere to go. When the brake is too hot the friction falls and the pedal goes soft: this is brake fade. The engine and the gearbox can slow the car without this heat, and the handbrake holds the car on a hill. A driver who believes the ABS stops the car in every condition will brake too late, because the system does nothing for a hot brake.
examples: On loose gravel a locked wheel digs into the surface, so the ABS is not always the shorter stop.
On ice the limit is the friction, not the braking system.
A tyre with a deep cut is a reason to change the tyre, not to rely on the ABS.
On a long descent I use a low gear, because hot brakes fade.
sections.heading: Where ABS does not help

terms.example: The road surface was loose gravel, so a locked wheel was the shorter stop.
terms.gloss: The material under the tyre: tarmac, concrete, gravel, sand, mud, snow, ice or leaves.

sections.body:
Five methods of braking are used in ordinary driving, and they solve different problems. Threshold braking and the anti-lock system both try to keep the wheel turning at the limit of grip; the difference is that one is done by the driver and the other by the system. Progressive braking asks for a smooth and early stop. Engine braking with a low gear asks the engine and the gearbox to slow the car. On a descent, the fifth method combines the engine and the brake so that the brakes stay cool.

The column that matters most to a driver is the last one. Every method has a surface on which it is weak, and the surface in front of the car decides which method to use. A method that is strong on a dry road is not necessarily strong on gravel or on ice, and no method is strong on every surface.

A driver who knows this table does not choose a method by habit. The driver checks the surface, the tyres and the load of the car, and then chooses. The manual of the car says what the brakes of that model can take.
examples: Threshold braking is the driver's own version of what the ABS does by itself.
I use progressive braking in traffic, because the stop is smooth and the tyres keep rolling.
On a descent I use a low gear, so that the brakes do not fade.
Every method has a surface on which it is weak.
sections.heading: The methods of braking, side by side

rows: Threshold braking (stamping) is braking at the limit of grip.
The driver presses the pedal hard and releases it as soon as the wheel starts to lock.
It keeps the wheel turning on a firm surface in a car without ABS, and it keeps the steering alive.
It needs the right timing, and on a loose surface it is easy to lock the wheel and lose the steering.
Anti-lock braking (ABS) is the system that manages the brake pressure.
The driver keeps the pedal down and the system reduces, holds or raises the brake pressure by itself.
It is strong on a firm or slippery surface, because it stops the wheel from locking without the driver having to guess.
It is weak on loose gravel, sand, mud, snow and leaves, where a locked wheel can be the shorter stop.
Progressive braking is a smooth and early stop.
The driver increases the pressure on the pedal steadily, without a sudden push.
It is strong in normal traffic and in rain, where it gives a smooth stop and keeps the tyres rolling.
It is weak in an emergency, because it takes too long to reach the full pressure.
Engine braking with a low gear is slowing the car with the engine.
The driver selects a low gear and lets the engine slow the car with the accelerator closed.
It is strong on a long descent, because it takes the heat out of the brakes.
It cannot stop the car quickly, and it does almost nothing at a low speed.
Braking on a descent with the engine is the way down a long hill.
The driver chooses a low gear before the descent, lets the engine hold the speed and uses the brake in short pushes.
It is strong on a long, steep descent, because it keeps the brakes from overheating and fading.
On a short descent it is unnecessary, and it takes attention and a low gear.

terms.example: In heavy traffic she used progressive braking and the stop was smooth.
terms.gloss: Applying the brake with steadily increasing pressure instead of one sudden push.

terms.example: On the long descent he used engine braking and the brakes stayed cool.
terms.gloss: Slowing the car with the engine and the gearbox instead of with the brake pedal.

sections.body:
Braking well is a habit of looking ahead, not a reflex at the last moment. The distance the car needs depends on the speed, the surface, the tyres, the load of the car and the time the driver's body takes to react. A wet road, a road covered with gravel and a road with ice on it each ask for more distance than a dry, clean road. The driver who knows this keeps a gap that can absorb a mistake.

In a car with anti-lock braking the technique is simple, and it is a technique of commitment: put the pedal down and keep it there. The system does the fine work of not locking the wheel. The one thing the driver must not do is pump the pedal, because every release tells the system to let the wheel turn and to drop the pressure.

In a car without anti-lock braking the driver does that fine work instead. The signal is in the pedal: when the pedal starts to go dead, the wheel is close to locking, and a small release brings it back. The steps below end with that move, so a reader can use the same list in either car.
examples: I keep the gap to the car in front so that I can stop in the road I can see.
I press the pedal down and keep it there; I do not pump it.
The pedal was going dead, so I released it a little and pressed again.
I steer around the obstacle while the car is still slowing.
sections.heading: How to brake well in a car with ABS
steps: Keep a gap to the car in front that lets you stop within the road you can see.
Look ahead and decide where the stop will happen, before the hazard reaches you.
Put the pedal down firmly and keep it down.
Do not pump the pedal yourself; hold it and let the system work.
Steer around the obstacle while the car is slowing, and keep the pedal down.
After the car has stopped, let the pedal come up and check the road and the traffic before you move.
In a car without ABS, press the pedal and, if it starts to go dead, release it a little and press again.

terms.example: The reaction time of the driver is part of the distance the car travels before the brakes work.
terms.gloss: The time between seeing a hazard and moving the brake pedal.

sections.body:
The handbrake still has a job. On ice or on loose gravel, a driver who needs to turn the car sharply may pull the handbrake to lock the rear wheels and let the car swing around. On gravel, the locked wheel digs into the surface and the car slows. This is a technique that needs practice, and it is not a replacement for a good tyre and a good gap.

On a long descent, engine braking is the safest way to lose speed, because the engine and the gearbox hold the car back and the brakes stay cool. The handbrake is also the last resort when the brake pedal does nothing: it can still stop the car, slowly.

Two things decide what is correct: the manual of the car and the road. The manual says what the handbrake and the gearbox do on that model. The road says what the surface can hold. Training matters more than the badge on the wheel. A driver who has practised a technique will use it well, and a driver who has only read the badge will not.
examples: On the ice I pulled the handbrake to lock the rear wheels.
On a long descent I use a low gear, so that the brakes do not fade.
If the pedal does nothing, the handbrake is the last resort.
The manual of the car and the road decide, not the badge on the wheel.
sections.heading: What the older methods are still good for

terms.example: She pulled the handbrake to lock the rear wheels on the ice.
terms.gloss: The lever beside the driver's seat that holds the car still; it is also called the parking brake.

sections.body:
Most of what a driver needs in this trade is the language of the road and of the workshop. Say what the car did, say how the pedal felt, and say what you want checked. Do not diagnose the fault yourself; describe the symptom and let the mechanic decide the cause.

A driving instructor needs to know what you felt and where. A colleague needs the rule and the reason. A mechanic needs the symptom in the order it happened, and the noise, the smell or the warning light that came with it.
examples: When I brake hard, the pedal starts to pulse under my foot. Is that normal?
The ABS light came on yesterday. The car still brakes, but I am keeping a bigger gap.
On the gravel road I brake by releasing the pedal, because a locked wheel digs in.
Do I stamp the pedal on this car, or is it fitted with ABS?
The pedal went soft on the long descent. I think the brakes faded.
I felt the pedal go dead just before the wheel locked, so I let it up and pressed again.
Is the front brake or the rear brake the one that locks first when I stop?
My instructor told me to look further ahead and to brake earlier on a wet road.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
The ABS warning light on the dashboard says one thing: the anti-lock braking system is not working as it should. The fault can be in a sensor, in a wiring circuit or in the control unit. The light does not mean that the car has no brakes, and it does not mean that the car cannot be driven.

The ordinary braking still works. The pedal still applies the brakes and the car still stops. What the driver has lost is the help that keeps a wheel from locking, so that the car can be steered around an obstacle while it slows. On some cars other brake aids are switched off as well when the light is on, and the pedal can feel different. The manual of the car says what happens on that model.

The driver has to change the way the car is driven. The gap to the car in front must be larger, and the braking must start earlier and be gentler, because the driver may have to release the pedal and press it again by hand when a wheel starts to lock. The speed on a wet road must come down. The car must be booked for a check, and the check is done before a long journey.

Two things are wrong: ignoring the light and driving as if the system were working, and keeping the usual speed on a wet road when the car can no longer be steered around a hazard. A car with the light on is still a car that brakes, but it is a car that needs a workshop and a longer gap.
examples: The ABS light is on, so I have booked the car for a check and I am keeping a bigger gap.
The car still brakes normally; the system that stops the wheels locking is the part that has failed.
I brake earlier and more gently until the car has been checked.
I did not ignore the light, and I did not drive on the wet motorway at my usual speed.
sections.heading: What to do when the ABS warning light comes on

item.summary: An anti-lock braking system is often taken as a promise that the car always stops in the same distance. It is not. After reading this you can describe how the system works, explain where it does not help, choose between threshold braking, progressive braking and engine braking, brake well with or without ABS, and say what to do when the warning light comes on.
item.title: ABS Is Not the Absolute Truth: The Limits of Anti-Lock Braking
